title: Agentic Reward Modeling: Verifying GUI Agent via Progressive Trajectory-Grounded Interaction
claim: Prior verification is either rigid and unscalable or passive and partially observed; ours adds active, trajectory-grounded tool interaction.
layout: 3 columns (a)-(c), top-to-bottom flow, shared task example, rightmost panel richer
description: Three side-by-side columns show how GUI agent verification evolved: (a) Rule-based Checking, (b) LLM-as-a-Judge, (c) Trajectory-Grounded Interaction. Each has a cartoon icon and a left-to-right arrow at the top. Below that, a vertical orange-outlined chain of icon boxes runs down the right side. In (a) it is Task, Execution, Create Scripts, Check. In (b) it is Task, Execution, Evaluation, Judge. In (c) it is Execution, Memory Consolidation, Interaction, Verify. Pastel yellow, red, blue and purple bands hold the stages. The first two columns share the same user task, a trajectory graph, and a code snippet or screenshot. Column (c) is denser. It has a verifier agent and a pipe-like toolbox with Judge Directly, Execute Shell, Env. Interaction, Check Screenshot and Execute Python. The final reward is YES/NO in (a) and (b). In (c) it adds a 'SURE!' confidence badge.
caption: The evolution of GUI agent verification methods. Unlike (a) Rule-based and (b) LLM-as-a-Judge approaches which suffer from scalability or partial observability issues, (c) Trajectory-Grounded Interactive Verification (VAGEN) instantiates a tool-augmented verifier agent capable of trajectory verification and environment interaction.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides a promising pathway for continuously advancing GUI agents, yet existing reward modeling paradigms face complementary limitations. Rule-based methods suffer from poor scalability and cannot handle open-ended tasks. LLM-as-a-Judge methods enable scalable trajectory verification but remain passive and are constrained by partial state observability, since key evidence often resides in latent environment states beyond the trajectory. Recent active environment interaction methods mitigate observability issues but tend to over-rely on probing while under-utilizing direct trajectory evidence, leading to verification inefficiency. To address these challenges, we advocate a trajectory-grounded interactive verification paradigm. We introduce VAGEN, a framework that employs a tool-augmented verifier agent governed by a Progressive Verification Mechanism, which follows a surface-to-latent and cheap-to-expensive design philosophy to extract trajectory evidence and probe environment states in a proactive end-to-end manner. Experiments on OSWorld-Verified and AndroidWorld benchmarks demonstrate that VAGEN significantly improves evaluation accuracy with a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off.
